question.text: Under the Negotiable Instruments Act 1881, a cheque is defined as:

answer.text: An instrument in writing containing an unconditional order to pay a certain sum of money to the bearer
An instrument in writing containing an unconditional promise to pay a certain sum of money
A bill of exchange drawn on a specified banker and not expressed to be payable otherwise than on demand
A negotiable instrument that can be drawn on any person and is payable on a specified future date

explanation.text: The Logic: The workbook defines a cheque as a bill of exchange drawn on a specified banker and not expressed to be payable otherwise than on demand. The two key features that distinguish a cheque from other negotiable instruments are that it must be drawn on a banker and must be payable on demand. The Trap: An instrument with an unconditional promise to pay describes a promissory note; an unconditional order to pay drawn on any person describes a bill of exchange. The cheque definition adds the two narrower requirements (drawn on a specified banker, payable on demand) that the other instruments do not share. Note: Source basis is p.361 of the NISM-Series-X-A Investment Adviser (Level 1) workbook (June 2025), where the definitions of cheque, promissory note, and bill of exchange appear together.
